reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
setup: A CMBS pool's properties earn net operating income (NOI) of USD 68m a year. Debt service on the notes is USD 54m a year. The pool's assets are worth about USD 5bn.
ask: NOI falls 25% and debt service stays the same. The DSCR ends up:

options.label: Still above 1.0
options.why: A DSCR of 1.26 means income covers debt service with 26% to spare, but that doesn't mean income can fall 26%. Income can only fall $1 - 1/1.26 \approx 20.6\%$ before coverage is lost, so a 25% fall goes past that point.

options.label: Unchanged, because DSCR depends on pool value
options.why: DSCR is a flow ratio: NOI divided by debt service. The USD 5bn pool value belongs in loan-to-value, not DSCR.

takeaway: A DSCR of $D$ lets income fall $1 - 1/D$ before cover is lost, not $D - 1$: at 1.26 that's about 21%, not 26%.

reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
setup: An MBS has four pools (USD m, coupon): apartments 24 at 8.4%, villas 32 at 7.0%, penthouses 16 at 6.8%, farmhouses 8 at 5.6%. The simple average of the four coupons is 6.95%.
ask: Will the balance-weighted WAC come out above the 6.95% simple average, below it, or about the same?

options.label: Below
options.why: For that, the low-coupon pools would have to be the big ones. Here the 8.4% and 7.0% pools hold 70% of the balance, so they pull the WAC up.

options.label: About the same
options.why: The weights are 30/40/20/10, nowhere near equal. Weighting moves the answer by about 0.3 percentage points.

takeaway: A weighted average leans toward its biggest pools. If the big pools have the high coupons, WAC sits above the simple average.

reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
setup: A commercial mortgage pool has four parts (USD m, days to maturity): superstores 26 at 82 days, offices 67 at 169 days, cinemas 22 at 253 days, restaurants 17 at 336 days. The simple average maturity is 210 days.
ask: Will the balance-weighted WAM come out above 210 days, below it, or about the same?

options.label: Above
options.why: The two long pools (253 and 336 days) hold only 29.5% of the balance. The office pool holds just over half, at 169 days, and it dominates.

options.label: About the same
options.why: With one pool at 51% of the balance, weighting matters. WAM comes out about 23 days below the simple average.

takeaway: Find the pool that holds most of the balance first: WAM sits just above its 169 days, well below the 210-day simple average.

reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
setup: A USD 1m portfolio holds 100 equal credits. Each has PD 3% and zero recovery, and default correlation is zero. The 95th percentile of the number of defaults is 4.
ask: The 95% credit VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1,000
options.why: Position-size slip: valued each credit at USD 1,000 instead of USD 1m / 100 = USD 10,000.

options.label: ≈ USD 3,000
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).

options.label: ≈ USD 40,000
options.why: That's the 95% quantile loss (4 defaults × USD 10,000). Credit VaR then subtracts the USD 30,000 expected loss.

takeaway: Credit VaR is the quantile loss minus expected loss. With 100 independent credits the 95th percentile is only one default above the mean.

reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
setup: A USD 1m portfolio holds 100 equal credits. Each has PD 3% and zero recovery, and default correlation is zero. The 95th percentile of the number of defaults is 4. So far you have: position size USD 10,000, and expected number of defaults $np = 3$.
ask: Which is larger: the 95% credit VaR or the expected loss?

options.label: Credit VaR
options.why: Credit VaR is only the loss beyond the mean: $(4 - 3) \times 10{,}000 = 10{,}000$. Expected loss is $3 \times 10{,}000 = 30{,}000$.

options.label: About equal
options.why: The quantile is 4 defaults and the mean is 3, so VaR covers one default and EL covers three. EL is three times VaR.

takeaway: In a granular, independent portfolio, credit VaR can be smaller than EL. EL is paid through the spread, and only the tail beyond it needs capital.

reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
setup: Portfolio Y has USD 1m notional across 30 positions, all exposures to the same obligor, so default correlation is 1. PD is 3% and recovery is zero.
ask: The 99% credit VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.03m
options.why: That's the expected loss ($0.03 \times 1\text{m}$). You stopped before subtracting it from the quantile loss.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.3m
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).

options.label: ≈ USD 29m
options.why: Treated each of the 30 positions as a USD 1m exposure: $30 \times (1 - 0.03)$. The portfolio can't lose more than its USD 1m notional.

working.label: P(no default)
working.display: $1 - 0.03 = 97\% < 99\%$, so the 99th percentile lands in the default state

takeaway: At correlation 1, the portfolio behaves like one loan. Compare $1 - PD$ with the confidence level: if the quantile falls in the default state, VaR is close to the full notional.

reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
setup: Portfolio Y has USD 1m notional across 30 positions, all exposures to the same obligor, so default correlation is 1. PD is 3% and recovery is zero. At 99% confidence, credit VaR is USD 970,000.
ask: The confidence level drops from 99% to 95%. Credit VaR:

options.label: Falls only slightly and stays near USD 0.9m
options.why: With $P(\text{no default}) = 97\% > 95\%$, the 95th percentile falls in the no-default state. The quantile loss is 0, so VaR is floored at zero.

options.label: Rises
options.why: A lower confidence level can never push a quantile up. Here it moves the quantile from the default state to the no-default state.

working.label: Where the 95th percentile sits
working.display: $97\% > 95\%$, so it falls in the no-default state (loss 0)

takeaway: With a single all-or-nothing credit, check whether $1 - PD$ is above or below the confidence level before computing anything: the answer is either close to the full notional or zero.

reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
setup: Two credits have PDs $\pi_1 = 0.025$ and $\pi_2 = 0.035$, and default correlation $\rho_{12} = 0.05$. The joint default probability is $\pi_{12} = \pi_1\pi_2 + \rho_{12}\sqrt{\pi_1(1-\pi_1)\,\pi_2(1-\pi_2)}$.
ask: Which term is larger: the independence term $\pi_1\pi_2$ or the correlation term?

options.label: The independence term
options.why: The product of two small PDs is tiny, at 0.0875%. The standard-deviation product is about 2.87%, so even a 0.05 correlation gives 0.1435%.

options.label: About equal
options.why: The correlation term is about 1.6 times the independence term. Even a small $\rho$ more than doubles the joint PD compared with independence.

takeaway: For small PDs, $\pi_1\pi_2$ is second-order small but the SD product is first-order. That's why even a tiny default correlation dominates the joint default probability.

reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
setup: Two credits have PDs $\pi_1 = 0.025$ and $\pi_2 = 0.035$, and default correlation $\rho_{12} = 0.05$.
ask: Their joint default probability is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip (0.1×).
That's just $\pi_1\pi_2$, the independence case. You dropped the correlation term.
Decimal slip on the correlation term, reading 0.001435 as 0.01435. The joint PD should sit near the independence value when $\rho$ is small.

takeaway: The joint PD must lie between $\pi_1\pi_2$ and $\min(\pi_1, \pi_2)$, and near the bottom of that range when $\rho$ is small.

reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
setup: Two credits have PDs $\pi_1 = 0.003$ and $\pi_2 = 0.004$. Capping the joint PD at $\min(\pi_1, \pi_2)$ gives a maximum permissible default correlation of 0.866.
ask: Credit 2's PD moves from 0.004 to 0.0035, closer to credit 1's. Credit 1 is unchanged. The maximum permissible default correlation:

options.label: Falls
options.why: The bound reaches 1 only when the two PDs are equal. Moving them closer relaxes the bound, from 0.866 to 0.926.

options.label: Unchanged, because the joint PD cap is still 0.003
options.why: The cap on $\pi_{12}$ is still 0.003, but the denominator $\sqrt{\pi_1(1-\pi_1)\pi_2(1-\pi_2)}$ shrinks as $\pi_2$ falls, so $\rho_{max}$ rises.

takeaway: Maximum default correlation is below 1 whenever the two PDs differ. It rises toward 1 as they converge.

reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
setup: Over the same horizon, a BBB credit has PD 0.003 and a CCC credit has PD 0.005. The probability that both default is 0.0002.
ask: The implied default correlation is closest to:

options.why: That's the joint default probability itself, not a correlation.
Scale slip (10×).
Divided by the product of the variances instead of the standard deviations (no square root). A correlation can't exceed 1.

takeaway: A joint PD 13 times the independence value implies a default correlation of only about 0.05. Low default correlations still cluster defaults a lot.

reading: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives: Credit Derivatives
setup: In a one-factor Gaussian copula, a firm has $\beta = 0.60$ and default threshold $k = -1.645$, so its unconditional PD is 5%. Its PD conditional on the market factor is $p(m) = N\!\left[\dfrac{k - \beta m}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\right]$.
ask: The economy turns down and $m = -1.41$. Compared with the 5% unconditional PD, the conditional PD is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Sign slip. With $m < 0$, the term $-\beta m = +0.846$ makes the numerator less negative, which pushes the PD up.

options.label: Unchanged, because $m$ only drives correlation
options.why: $m$ enters the conditional PD directly. Only at $m = 0$ does $p(m) = N(k) = 5\%$.

takeaway: In the one-factor copula a negative $m$ raises the conditional PD. The check: $m = 0$ gives back $N(k)$.

reading: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives: Credit Derivatives
setup: In a one-factor Gaussian copula, a firm has $\beta = 0.60$ and default threshold $k = -1.645$, so its unconditional PD is 5%. Its PD conditional on the market factor is $p(m) = N\!\left[\dfrac{k - \beta m}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\right]$. The market factor falls to $m = -1.41$.
ask: The conditional PD is closest to:

options.why: Sign slip on the factor term: $(k + \beta m)/0.8 = -3.11$ gives $N = 0.09\%$. A downturn can't lower the PD below the unconditional 5%.
Scale slip (0.1×).
That's the unconditional PD, $N(k)$. It ignores the $m = -1.41$ shock.

takeaway: A 1.4σ downturn with β = 0.6 roughly triples a 5% PD. Conditioning on $m$ is how the model makes defaults cluster.

reading: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives: Credit Derivatives
setup: In a one-factor Gaussian copula, a firm has $\beta = 0.60$ and default threshold $k = -1.645$, so its unconditional PD is 5%. Its PD conditional on the market factor is $p(m) = N\!\left[\dfrac{k - \beta m}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\right]$. With $m = -1.41$ you have the numerator $k - \beta m = -0.799$. A colleague divides it by $1 - \beta^2 = 0.64$ instead of $\sqrt{1-\beta^2} = 0.80$.
ask: Compared with the correct conditional PD, the colleague's figure is:

options.label: Too high
options.why: Dividing a negative numerator by a smaller number makes the argument more negative ($-1.25$ vs $-1.00$), so $N(\cdot)$ gets smaller.

options.label: The same, because the scaling cancels
options.why: Nothing cancels. The divisor sets how many standard deviations the threshold sits from the conditional mean.

takeaway: The idiosyncratic part has standard deviation $\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$, not variance $1-\beta^2$. Using the variance understates a stressed PD.

reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
setup: US municipal defaults arrive as a Poisson process with an average of 6.0 per year.
ask: The probability that the next default happens within one month is closest to:

options.why: Converted to monthly twice: $\lambda t = 6/12/12 = 0.042$.
Scale slip (0.3×).
Forgot the time conversion. With $t = 1$ year, $1 - e^{-6} = 99.8\%$.

takeaway: Half a default is expected per month, so a 30–40% chance of at least one is the right size.

reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
setup: Municipal defaults arrive as a Poisson process at 6.0 per year. Over one month, $\lambda t = 6.0 \times 1/12 = 0.5$.
ask: Is the probability of at least one default within the month above 50%, below it, or exactly 50%?

options.label: Exactly 50%
options.why: $\lambda t$ is the expected number of defaults, not a probability. For $x > 0$, $1 - e^{-x} < x$.

options.label: Above 50%
options.why: $e^{-0.5} = 60.7\%$ is the survival probability, the chance of no default. The default probability is the other 39.3%.

takeaway: $1 - e^{-\lambda t}$ is always below $\lambda t$. The expected count overstates the probability of at least one event.

reading: Reading 87: Rating Migration Matrices and Default Probability Measures
setup: Moody's average cumulative default rates for Caa-C: 36.908% by year 3 and 44.128% by year 4.
ask: Which is larger: the year-4 marginal PD (seen from today) or the year-4 PD conditional on surviving to the end of year 3?

options.label: The marginal PD
options.why: The conditional PD divides the marginal by the survival probability, 0.631. Dividing by less than 1 makes it bigger.

options.label: About equal
options.why: They'd match only if survival to year 3 were close to 100%. For Caa it's only 63%.

takeaway: Conditional PD is marginal PD divided by survival, so it's always at least the marginal, and much larger for weak credits.

reading: Reading 87: Rating Migration Matrices and Default Probability Measures
setup: Moody's average cumulative default rates for Caa-C: 36.908% by year 3 and 44.128% by year 4.
ask: The PD for year 4, conditional on no earlier default, is closest to:

options.why: Percent-vs-decimal slip (a factor of 100).
Scale slip (0.3×).
That's the four-year cumulative PD: default at any time in years 1–4, not in year 4 alone.

takeaway: Cumulative, then difference, then divide by survival. About one in nine Caa bonds still alive after year 3 defaults in year 4.

reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
setup: One-year migration matrix, where default (D) is absorbing. From A: to A 0.90, to B 0.09, to D 0.01. From B: to A 0.05, to B 0.85, to D 0.10. A credit is rated A today.
ask: Of the two year-2 default paths, A→A→D and A→B→D, which adds more to the two-year PD?

options.label: A→A→D, staying in A
options.why: $0.90 \times 0.01 = 0.90\%$. But the rare downgrade meets a PD 10 times higher: $0.09 \times 0.10 = 0.90\%$ as well.

options.label: A→B→D, through the downgrade
options.why: Close, but not bigger: both paths come to exactly 0.90%.

takeaway: Migration isn't second-order: a small downgrade probability times a much higher PD can match the stay-put path. That's why the two-year PD is above twice the one-year PD.

reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
setup: GlobalTech's 5-year CDS spread is 240bp and expected recovery is 40%. Its bonds trade near par with 3y/5y/10y spreads of 50/60/100bp. Assume a constant hazard rate, with $s \approx \lambda(1-R)$.
ask: Is the implied hazard rate higher than the 240bp CDS spread, lower, or equal to it?

options.label: Lower
options.why: Slip: multiplied by LGD instead of dividing. A spread pays for loss, so dividing by $1 - R = 0.6$ scales it up.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only if recovery were zero. With 40% recovery, each default costs 60%, so more defaults are needed to justify the spread.

takeaway: $\lambda = s/(1-R)$: the hazard rate is always at least the spread, because each default loses only a fraction of par.

reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
setup: GlobalTech's 5-year CDS spread is 240bp. With a 40% recovery assumption, the implied constant hazard rate is $\lambda = s/(1-R) = 4.0\%$.
ask: Keep the spread at 240bp but assume 60% recovery instead. The implied hazard rate:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Higher recovery means each default costs less, so more frequent defaults are needed to justify the same spread: $0.024/0.40 = 6.0\%$.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: $\lambda$ depends on LGD directly. Only CVA with the same $R$ used on both sides is roughly recovery-neutral.

takeaway: For a fixed spread, a higher recovery assumption means a higher implied default intensity.

reading: Reading 88: Hull, Estimating Default Probabilities
setup: GlobalTech's 5-year CDS spread is 240bp and expected recovery is 40%. Its bonds trade near par with 3y/5y/10y spreads of 50/60/100bp. Assume a constant hazard rate, with $s \approx \lambda(1-R)$.
ask: The 5-year cumulative default probability is closest to:

options.why: Multiplied the spread by $(1 - R)$ instead of dividing, and stopped at one year.
That's the annual hazard rate. You stopped before applying the 5-year horizon.
Scale slip (3×).

takeaway: Spread over LGD gives the annual intensity. Over $T$ years the cumulative PD is $1 - e^{-\lambda T}$, a bit under $\lambda T$.

reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
setup: Two-way CSA. The dealer's exposure to the counterparty is USD 48m. The counterparty owes an independent amount of USD 5m and has a threshold of USD 20m. The dealer already holds USD 29.5m of collateral after haircuts. The minimum transfer amount (MTA) is USD 1m.
ask: The resulting margin call is:

options.label: The dealer must return collateral
options.why: The requirement is $48 + 5 - 20 = 33$. That exceeds the 29.5 held, so the counterparty is short, not over-collateralised.

options.label: The counterparty must post more collateral
No transfer, because the gap is inside the MTA
options.why: The gap is USD 3.5m, well above the USD 1m MTA.

takeaway: Independent amount adds, threshold subtracts. Net against collateral already held, then test against the MTA.

reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
setup: Two-way CSA: exposure USD 48m, independent amount USD 5m, threshold USD 20m, collateral held USD 29.5m after haircuts, MTA USD 1m. Right now the counterparty owes a delivery of USD 3.5m.
ask: The threshold is renegotiated from USD 20m to USD 25m, with everything else unchanged. The margin call:

options.label: Flips, and the dealer must return collateral
Shrinks, but the counterparty still posts
options.why: Raising the threshold cuts the requirement by the full USD 5m: $3.5 - 5 = -1.5$. The dealer now holds USD 1.5m too much, which is above the MTA.

options.label: Grows
options.why: The threshold is subtracted from exposure, so raising it lowers the requirement.

takeaway: A threshold change moves the call one-for-one. If the old call was smaller than the change, the direction flips.

reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
setup: One-way CSA with no threshold. The requirement is the bank's full exposure of USD 62m, and the MTA is USD 0.5m. No collateral is held yet. The hedge fund offers USD 40m of government bonds (4% haircut) and USD 25m of corporate bonds (12% haircut), which is USD 65m at market value.
ask: After haircuts, the position is:

options.label: A surplus
options.why: At market value it's +3.0m, but the haircuts take off $1.6 + 3.0 = 4.6$m. That leaves 60.4m of credit against the 62m required.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The −1.6m gap is clear, and more than three times the 0.5m MTA.

takeaway: Haircuts only ever reduce the collateral credit. A 3m surplus at market value can turn into a shortfall once 4.6m of haircuts come off.

reading: Reading 95: Gregory, Collateral and Margin
setup: One-way CSA with no threshold. The requirement is the bank's full exposure of USD 62m, and the MTA is USD 0.5m. The hedge fund offers USD 40m of government bonds (4% haircut) and USD 25m of corporate bonds (12% haircut), which is USD 65m at market value.
ask: The total haircut deduction, meaning market value minus collateral credit given, is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1.6m
options.why: Applied only the government-bond haircut ($40 \times 4\%$) and forgot the corporate leg.

options.label: ≈ USD 14m
options.why: Scale slip (3×).

options.label: ≈ USD 46m
options.why: Percent-vs-decimal slip: read the 4% and 12% haircuts as 0.4 and 1.2.

takeaway: Size the haircut first: 4.6m against a 3m headline surplus tells you the sign of the answer.

reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
setup: A netting set is simulated at four annual points (USD m). Expected MtM: +2, +1, −1, −3. Expected exposure (EE): 5, 7, 6, 3. 97.5% PFE: 14, 19, 16, 9.
ask: Maximum exposure over the four years is closest to:

options.why: That's the peak expected MtM. Exposure is floored at zero path by path, and the maximum is taken from the PFE column.
That's the peak EE, the mean profile. Maximum exposure is the worst case, read from the PFE profile.
Added the four PFEs together. Maximum exposure is the largest single PFE, not their sum.

takeaway: Maximum exposure is the peak of the PFE profile, well above any EE.

reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
setup: A netting set is simulated at four annual points (USD m). Expected MtM: +2, +1, −1, −3. Expected exposure (EE): 5, 7, 6, 3. 97.5% PFE: 14, 19, 16, 9. Effective EE is the running maximum of EE.
ask: Which is larger: EPE (the time average of EE) or effective EPE?

options.label: EPE
options.why: The running maximum can never fall below EE, so effective EPE is always at least EPE.

options.label: Equal
options.why: They're equal only if EE never declines. Here EE falls after year 2, and the running maximum locks in 7.

takeaway: Effective EPE ≥ EPE, and the gap is strictly positive as soon as the EE profile turns down.

reading: Reading 83: Doumpos, Fundamentals of Credit Risk
setup: A bank has Tier 1 capital of USD 200m, Tier 2 capital of USD 100m and risk-weighted assets of USD 2bn.
ask: The capital adequacy (total capital) ratio is closest to:

options.why: Tier 2 on its own over RWA. Tier 2 is never used alone as a capital adequacy measure.
Tier 2 divided by Tier 1. That describes the capital mix, not capital adequacy.
Scale slip (10×), for example reading RWA as USD 200m instead of USD 2bn.

takeaway: CAR, the Tier 1 ratio and the CET1 ratio all divide by RWA. Only the numerator changes.

reading: Reading 83: Doumpos, Fundamentals of Credit Risk
setup: A bank has Tier 1 capital of USD 200m, Tier 2 capital of USD 100m and risk-weighted assets of USD 2bn. Its total capital ratio is 15% and its Tier 1 ratio is 10%.
ask: The bank issues USD 50m of Tier 2 subordinated debt, and RWA doesn't change. Its Tier 1 ratio:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Only the total capital ratio rises, to 17.5%. The Tier 1 ratio's numerator excludes Tier 2 entirely.

options.label: Falls
options.why: RWA is unchanged and Tier 1 is unchanged, so nothing pushes the ratio down.

takeaway: The capital ratios share a denominator. Check which numerator the new capital actually enters.

reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
setup: A portfolio has MtM +15. You hold variation margin of 10, and each side has posted segregated initial margin of 6. Ignore close-out costs.
ask: Before the zero floor, is the counterparty-credit residual $MtM - VM_{held} - IM_{held}$ positive, negative or zero?

options.label: Positive
options.why: Dropped the initial margin held: $15 - 10 = 5$. The IM you hold is also a buffer against the counterparty defaulting.

options.label: Zero
options.why: $15 - 10 - 6 = -1$. The position is slightly over-collateralised.

working.label: Funding exposure
working.display: $15 - 10 + 6 = 11$ (posted IM is locked away and must be funded)

takeaway: Initial margin held reduces credit exposure. Segregated initial margin posted adds to funding exposure. Same number, opposite signs.

reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
setup: A portfolio has MtM +15. You hold variation margin of 10. Each side has posted segregated initial margin of 6, which can't be reused. Counterparty credit exposure is 0 and funding exposure is 11.
ask: Both sides raise their segregated initial margin from 6 to 8. Your funding exposure:

options.label: Falls
options.why: IM held reduces credit exposure. IM you post that is segregated must be funded, so it adds to funding exposure.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Credit exposure stays at its floor of 0, but funding exposure goes from 11 to 13.

takeaway: More segregated IM reduces counterparty risk but costs funding. That trade-off is what MVA prices.

reading: Reading 94: Gregory, ISDA Master Agreement, Netting and Close-out
setup: Three swaps on identical terms, each listed as fixed payer → fixed receiver: (1) Bank A → Bank B, USD 250m; (2) Bank B → Bank C, USD 180m; (3) Bank C → Bank A, USD 130m. Count paying fixed as + and receiving fixed as −.
ask: Across its two swaps, Bank B's net fixed-rate position is:

options.label: Flat, since B sits in the middle of the chain
options.why: B receives fixed on 250 (from A) and pays fixed on only 180 (to C). That nets to receiving 70, not zero.

options.label: A net payer of fixed
options.why: Sign slip. B pays on 180 but receives on 250.

working.label: Notional after compression
working.display: A pays fixed on 120 in total (70 to B, 50 to C), down from 560 gross

takeaway: Net every bank with a fixed sign convention. The nets must sum to zero, and a middle-of-the-chain bank isn't flat unless its two notionals match.

reading: Reading 94: Gregory, ISDA Master Agreement, Netting and Close-out
setup: Three swaps on identical terms, each listed as fixed payer → fixed receiver: (1) Bank A → Bank B, USD 250m; (2) Bank B → Bank C, USD 180m; (3) Bank C → Bank A, USD 130m. A multilateral compression cuts gross notional from USD 560m to USD 120m.
ask: After compression, each bank's net interest-rate exposure is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Compression removes redundant gross notional. Each bank's net position, and so its rate risk, is kept exactly.

options.label: Higher
options.why: No bank's net fixed position changes, so rate risk can't increase.

takeaway: Compression lowers notional, operational load and leverage exposure. Market risk is unchanged.

reading: Fabozzi, Securitisation Cash Flows and Structures
setup: A pool prepaid 0.55% of its scheduled balance this month (SMM). Multiplying by 12 gives 6.60%.
ask: Is the compounded annual rate $CPR = 1 - (1 - SMM)^{12}$ higher than 6.60%, lower, or equal?

options.label: Higher
options.why: Survival compounds: each month's prepayment applies to a smaller surviving balance, so 12 × SMM overstates the annual rate.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only to first order. The compounding shortfall is about 0.2 percentage points here.

takeaway: Annualising a monthly rate by compounding survival always gives less than 12 times the rate. It's the same idea as a hazard rate against a cumulative PD.

reading: Fabozzi, Securitisation Cash Flows and Structures
setup: A pool 20 months seasoned prepaid 0.55% of its balance this month (SMM), which is a CPR of 6.40%. The 100 PSA benchmark ramps CPR up by 0.2% a month to 6% at month 30, then stays flat.
ask: Relative to 100 PSA, this pool is prepaying:

options.label: Slower
options.why: At month 20 the benchmark is only $6\% \times 20/30 = 4.00\%$. A CPR of 6.40% beats it.

options.label: At about 100 PSA
options.why: 6.40% is close to the terminal 6%, but the benchmark at month 20 is 4.00%: $6.40/4.00 = 160$ PSA.

takeaway: PSA is a ramp: compare with the benchmark at the pool's seasoning month, not with the 6% plateau.

reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
setup: CVA on an uncollateralised swap uses a hazard rate implied from the counterparty's CDS spread, $\lambda \approx s/(1-R)$. The same recovery $R$ also sets the loss given default in CVA. The EPE profile is fixed.
ask: The recovery assumption rises from 40% to 60% and the CDS spread doesn't move. CVA:

options.label: Falls
options.why: LGD does fall, but the implied $\lambda$ rises by the same factor. The two $(1-R)$ terms cancel.

options.label: Rises
options.why: The higher implied default intensity is exactly offset by the smaller loss per default.

working.label: Result
working.display: No $R$ left, so CVA is about recovery-neutral (if the same $R$ is used both times)

takeaway: CVA rises with the spread but hardly moves with recovery, because $R$ enters twice with opposite signs.

reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
setup: Two securitisations have identical tranche attachment points. Both pools hold assets with a 2% individual PD. Pool 1's pairwise default correlation is 0.05 and Pool 2's is 0.40.
ask: For the same senior rating, Pool 2's senior tranche needs subordination that is:

options.label: The same, since expected loss is identical
options.why: Expected loss is the same, but correlation fattens the tail. The tail is what reaches the senior tranche.

options.label: Smaller
options.why: Higher correlation makes defaults cluster, which raises the chance of breaching any attachment point.

working.label: Senior tranche
working.display: Higher chance of breaching the attachment point, so more subordination is needed

takeaway: PD moves the whole loss distribution. Correlation moves only its shape, and the shape is what sets senior subordination.

reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
setup: A credit portfolio's PDs, exposures and LGDs are all held fixed. Pairwise default correlation between the obligors rises.
ask: The portfolio's expected loss:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Correlation raises unexpected loss and credit VaR, not EL. $EL = \sum PD_i \cdot EAD_i \cdot LGD_i$ has no correlation term.

options.label: Falls
options.why: EL is linear in the individual PDs, and none of them changed.

takeaway: Correlation moves the tail (UL, credit VaR, capital), not the mean (EL, spread).

reading: Reading 88: Malz, Credit VaR
setup: A portfolio of BBB bonds is managed over one year. It switches from buy-and-hold to monthly rebalancing: any bond downgraded below BBB is sold and replaced with a BBB bond.
ask: The probability of large default losses (the far tail):

options.label: Rises
options.why: Rebalancing does make small downgrade losses realised and more frequent. But it cuts off the migration path that leads to default.

options.label: Unchanged, since the average rating is BBB either way
options.why: The average rating is the same, but the loss distribution isn't: rebalancing gives a shorter tail and a thicker body.

working.label: Path to default
working.display: Credits reach default by migrating downward, and rebalancing sells them on the first downgrade

working.label: Tail
working.display: Default losses in the portfolio become much rarer

working.label: Body
working.display: Every downgrade is realised as a small permanent loss

takeaway: Constant-risk rebalancing trades tail risk for more frequent small losses.

reading: Reading 83: Doumpos, Fundamentals of Credit Risk
setup: For one rating category, a risk manager backs default probabilities out of corporate bond spreads with $\lambda = s/(1-R)$ and compares them with historical default rates.
ask: Compared with the historical PDs, the spread-implied PDs are typically:

options.label: Lower
options.why: The spread carries liquidity and systematic-risk premia on top of expected default loss, and $s/(1-R)$ counts all of it as default.

options.label: About the same
options.why: The gap is large, often several times, and widest for high-grade issuers where the premia dwarf the expected loss.

working.label: Implied PD
working.display: Counts the whole spread as default compensation, so it's inflated compared with the real-world PD

takeaway: Risk-neutral PDs are above real-world PDs. Use risk-neutral for valuation and CVA, real-world for loss forecasting and capital.

reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
setup: A bank has a currency swap and an interest-rate swap with one counterparty under a single enforceable netting agreement.
ask: The correlation between the two trades' values moves from strongly positive to strongly negative. The netting benefit:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Netting pays off when trade values have opposite signs, and negative correlation makes that the usual state.

options.label: Unchanged, since netting is a legal mechanism
options.why: The legal right is the same, but how much it saves depends on how often the trades offset each other.

working.label: Strong positive correlation
working.display: Values usually share a sign, so the benefit is small

working.label: Strong negative correlation
working.display: Values usually offset, so the benefit is largest

takeaway: Netting benefit is largest for negatively correlated trades and close to zero for strongly positive ones.

reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
setup: An investment firm trades derivatives in volatile markets under a collateral agreement that remargins every 3 days.
ask: The remargining period is cut from 3 days to 1 day. Residual uncollateralised exposure:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Less time passes between calls, so the position has less room to move against the firm before collateral arrives.

options.label: Unchanged, because the threshold and MTA fix it
options.why: The threshold and MTA add to residual exposure, and so does the move over the margin period of risk, which scales with $\sqrt{\tau}$.

takeaway: Shorter remargining means a shorter margin period of risk. The exposure that builds up in that window shrinks roughly with $\sqrt{\tau}$.

reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
setup: At a future date, a netting set has three equally likely values: +12, 0 and −12.
ask: Which is larger: the expected MtM or the expected exposure?

options.label: Equal, because the distribution is symmetric
options.why: Exposure floors each scenario at zero before averaging, so the −12 counts as 0, not −12.

options.label: Expected MtM
options.why: Expected exposure averages non-negative numbers, so it can't be below the expected MtM.

takeaway: $EE = E[\max(V, 0)] \ge \max(E[V], 0)$. The floor goes inside the expectation.
